aAbout: N2YO is a satellite-tracking website: ISS and satellite positions calculated from TLE data, displayed on tracking maps with tables, pass predictions for your location, a large satellite catalogue with categories and technical details, and a documented API for developers. It tracks objects in orbit only — no flights, ships, cameras or weather. It is free to use, supported by advertising, and its API is offered with an API key. For satellite spotters and amateur-radio users planning around a specific object or pass, it has long been one of the default bookmarks.
aStrengths: N2YO is the deeper live-tracking tool: TLE-based positions for a large satellite catalogue, a tracking map for following an object as it orbits, a satellite database organised by category, and a documented API so developers and radio users can pull positions and pass predictions into their own tools. For anyone who wants to follow satellites continuously — not just catch one visible pass — that catalogue-plus-API depth has no equivalent on the other side of this comparison.
bAbout: Heavens-Above, run by Heavens-Above GmbH, is a satellite-visibility prediction website organised around your location. It publishes 10-day predictions for satellites of special interest — individually listed objects including the ISS, CSS (Tianhe), HST and others — with visible-pass tables giving brightness (magnitude), start, highest-point and end times in altitude and azimuth, plus a star chart for each pass. It adds daily predictions for brighter satellites, Starlink pass predictions, a satellite database, amateur-radio satellite passes, a live sky chart, a current ISS position, and an interactive 3D visualisation of the ISS. Login is explicitly optional — the site works for an anonymous user — and no paywall was found on the pages checked. Its official Android app is free with ads, with a Pro app to remove them. It offers no webcams, flights or ships.
bStrengths: Heavens-Above is the precision instrument for actually seeing a satellite with your own eyes: 10-day, location-based visible-pass tables that tell you how bright a pass will be and exactly where and when to look, in altitude and azimuth, with a star chart drawn for that specific pass. Add daily brighter-satellite predictions with a brightness filter, Starlink predictions, amateur-radio passes and a live sky chart — all with no account required — and for the backyard observer planning tonight's sky, it answers the question more completely than any tracking map.
betterAnswer: They answer different questions. N2YO answers 'where is it now, and where is it going?' — a live TLE-based tracking map, a deep satellite catalogue and an API for developers and radio users. Heavens-Above answers 'when can I see it from here?' — 10-day visible-pass predictions for your exact location, with brightness, altitude-azimuth times and a star chart for each pass. If you follow satellites on a screen or in code, use N2YO; if you go outside and look up, check Heavens-Above first.

Heavens-Above centres on visibility: 10-day predictions for your location showing whether a pass will be visible, how bright it will be, and where to look, with a star chart per pass. Both predict passes; each is built around a different half of the hobby.
faqs.q: What is the main difference between N2YO and Heavens-Above?

faqs.a: Heavens-Above. Its ISS visible-pass tables give brightness (magnitude) and start, highest-point and end times in altitude and azimuth for your location, with a star chart for each individual pass — exactly what you need standing outside. N2YO also calculates pass predictions for your location, but its strength is tracking and catalogue depth rather than per-pass viewing charts.

intro: N2YO and Heavens-Above are the two classic satellite-watching sites, bookmarked by a generation of ISS spotters — and they start from opposite ends of the same question. N2YO starts with the orbit: live TLE-based positions on tracking maps, a large satellite catalogue and a documented API. Heavens-Above starts with your backyard: precise, location-based predictions of which passes you can actually see, how bright they will be, and where in the sky to look, complete with star charts. Both are free; neither requires an account to do its main job.

verdictA: Choose N2YO if you want to follow satellites on a map or in code — live TLE-based positions, a deep catalogue, pass predictions and a documented API, free with ads.
verdictB: Choose Heavens-Above if your question is 'what can I see tonight, and when?' — 10-day visible-pass tables with brightness and star charts for your exact location, no account needed.
verdictLine: N2YO watches the orbit; Heavens-Above watches your sky. N2YO is the tracker — live positions, catalogue and API. Heavens-Above is the observer's almanac — whether a pass is visible, how bright, and where to look. Most serious satellite watchers end up using both, for different moments.
worldEye: Both sites look only at orbit — neither shows you the ground the satellites are passing over. WorldEye is the ground-level complement: a hosted 3D globe that opens free in any browser with no signup — 74,229 public cameras across 109 countries, with live satellites in the same view as flights, ships, weather, earthquakes and wildfires. It does not match N2YO's catalogue or API, or Heavens-Above's per-pass brightness tables and star charts, and it makes no such claim. Its Pro tier is $7.99/week, $13.99/month or $74.99/year for viewers who want more of the globe.
